about.title: Linear Inequalities in Two Variables
about.length_note: About 30 minutes fits. The lesson teaches one idea per step: what a solution is, the boundary line, solid or dashed, the test point, shading, then a money limit. Each step has a short check question. Learners who want more time can pause after any question.

say.text: Welcome back. In class 14 you graphed lines like y = x + 1. Today we graph a whole region instead of just a line.
Here is the idea. A linear inequality in two variables looks like a line equation, but with <, >, ≤ or ≥ in place of the equals sign.

show.text: Inequality in two variables: x + y ≤ 5

say.text: A solution is a pair (x, y) that makes it true. Try (2, 3) in x + y ≤ 5. 2 + 3 is 5, and 5 ≤ 5 is true. So (2, 3) is a solution.

show.text: Test (2, 3): 2 + 3 = 5 | 5 ≤ 5 is TRUE | so (2, 3) is a solution

ask.q: Which pair is a solution of x + y ≤ 5?
ask.why: 1 + 3 = 4, and 4 ≤ 5 is true. The other pairs add up to 7, 6 and 6, which are all more than 5.

say.text: There are endless solutions, so we can't list them. We draw them. The graph shades every point that works.

show.text: A coordinate plane with a diagonal line running across it. One side of the line is shaded light blue. The other side is left white.

say.text: Step one is the boundary line. Change the inequality sign to an equals sign and graph that line. For y > x + 1, graph y = x + 1.

show.text: y > x + 1 | boundary: y = x + 1 | start at (0, 1), go up 1 and right 1 | points (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)

say.text: Step two is solid or dashed. If the sign is ≤ or ≥, points on the line count, so draw it solid. If the sign is < or >, points on the line don't count, so draw it dashed.

show.text: SOLID line: ≤ and ≥ (line is included) || DASHED line: < and > (line is not included)

ask.q: What kind of boundary line does y < 2x + 3 get?
ask.right: Dashed, because < does not include the line
wrong: Solid, because it has a line in it
ask.why: Only ≤ and ≥ include the points on the line. A plain < or > leaves the line dashed.

say.text: Step three is the test point. The line cuts the plane into two sides. Pick any point that is not on the line and put it into the original inequality.

show.text: Test point: a point off the line, plugged into the inequality

say.text: If the test point makes it true, shade that side. If it makes it false, shade the other side. The point (0, 0) is easiest, so use it when you can.

show.text: TRUE: shade the side with the test point || FALSE: shade the other side

say.text: Let's do the whole thing for y > x + 1. We draw it dashed. Test (0, 0): is 0 > 0 + 1? That's 0 > 1, which is false.

show.text: y > x + 1 | dashed line y = x + 1 | test (0, 0): 0 > 1 is FALSE | shade the side WITHOUT (0, 0): above the line

ask.q: For y > x + 1, the test point (0, 0) gave a false statement. What do we do?
ask.right: Shade the side of the line that does not contain (0, 0)
ask.why: False means (0, 0) is not a solution, so its side is not part of the answer. We shade the other side.

say.text: Always double-check. Pick a point in the shaded area, like (0, 3). Is 3 > 0 + 1? Yes, 3 > 1, so the shading is right.
Now one with a solid line: 2x + 3y ≤ 12. The line crosses the axes at (6, 0) and (0, 4). Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 12 is true, so shade the side with the origin.

show.text: 2x + 3y ≤ 12 | solid line through (6, 0) and (0, 4) | test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 12 is TRUE | shade the side WITH (0, 0)

say.text: One warning. Try y ≥ 2x. This line passes through (0, 0), so (0, 0) is on the line and is not a good test point. Pick another point, like (1, 0).

show.text: y ≥ 2x | solid line through (0, 0) | (0, 0) is ON the line, so don't use it | test (1, 0): 0 ≥ 2 is FALSE | shade the other side, above the line

ask.q: For y ≥ 2x, which point is a bad choice for a test point?
ask.right: (0, 0), because it is on the line
ask.why: The point (0, 0) sits on the boundary line, so it can't tell you which side to shade. The other points are off the line.

say.text: Now real life. Sam has $20 for a game store. Skins cost $4 each and boosts cost $2 each. With x skins and y boosts, the money limit is 4x + 2y ≤ 20.
The boundary line goes through (5, 0) and (0, 10). It's solid, because spending exactly $20 is allowed. Test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 20 is true, so shade toward the origin.

show.text: 4x + 2y ≤ 20 | solid line through (5, 0) and (0, 10) | test (0, 0): 0 ≤ 20 TRUE | shade toward the origin

ask.q: Sam wants 3 skins and 4 boosts. Is that allowed by 4x + 2y ≤ 20?
ask.right: Yes. It costs 12 + 8 = 20, which is exactly $20, and the line is solid
wrong: No, because it is on the line
No, because it costs more than $20
ask.why: 4(3) + 2(4) = 20, and 20 ≤ 20 is true. Points on a solid line count as solutions.

say.text: Limits like time and money also have a catch. You can't buy a negative number of skins, so only the part where x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 makes sense. Skins also come in whole numbers, so the real answers are dots, not every point in the shaded area.

show.text: Real-world limits: x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 (no negatives) | whole items: only the dots count | time works the same way: x + y ≤ 60 minutes

say.text: Let's put the steps together. Boundary line, solid or dashed, test point, shade. Then check one point in the shading.

show.text: 1. Graph the boundary line (change the sign to =) | 2. Solid for ≤ ≥, dashed for < > | 3. Test a point that is not on the line | 4. True: shade that side. False: shade the other side

ask.q: A graph has a dashed boundary line, and the region above the line is shaded. Which inequality could it be?
ask.why: The line is dashed, so the sign is > or <, not ≥ or ≤. Shading above means y is bigger than the line, so it is >.

other_side.claim: Use a test point to decide which side to shade.
other_side.other_view: Many courses teach a shortcut. Solve for y, then shade above for y > or y ≥, and below for y < or y ≤. This is quick, but it goes wrong if you forget to flip the sign when dividing by a negative number. It also doesn't work for vertical lines like x > 3, which have no y to solve for. The test point works every time, so this lesson uses it, and the shortcut makes a good second check.
